title: Novel Potential Plasma Biomarkers: Exercise-Specific Proteomic Signatures in the Plasma of Racehorses during Training Adaptations and Racing Efforts
projectDescription: Background:  Racehorses undergo profound physiological changes in response to training and competition, yet current tools to assess training adaptation and overload remain limited. Traditional biomarkers often fail to reflect the complex molecular dynamics induced by physical effort. This study aimed to identify new plasma biomarkers of exercise adaptation in racehorses using high-throughput proteomics. Objectives: We hypothesized that systematic training and racing efforts induce distinct proteomic signatures in plasma, enabling the identification of novel candidate biomarkers reflecting training status, oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolic remodeling. Study Design: This was an in vivo longitudinal study using repeated blood sampling in the same horses across different phases of training and racing. Methods: Forty-nine Arabian and Thoroughbred racehorses underwent standardized high-intensity training. Plasma samples were collected at rest, immediately post-exercise, and after recovery, during three phases: early training (T1), mid-season conditioning (T2), and racing (R). A total of 314 samples were analyzed using TMT-based quantitative proteomics and high-resolution mass spectrometry. Protein expression changes were evaluated with statistical correction for multiple comparisons (FDR < 0.05), and functional pathway enrichment was conducted via STRING and ShinyGO. Results: The proteomic response evolved across phases: T1 revealed a broad activation of inflammatory (S100A8/A9), antioxidant (SOD1, catalase), and metabolic proteins (G6PD, PGK1), while T2 showed refined expression of remodeling and redox regulators (decorin, thymosin β4, glutathione S-transferase). The racing phase induced the strongest response, with >100 upregulated proteins involved in energy metabolism, oxidative stress defense, and cytoskeletal adaptation. Several proteins (e.g., S100A8, thymosin β4, prothymosin α, cofilin-1, lipocalins) consistently changed across all phases, indicating their biomarker potential. Conclusions: This study identified a panel of promising plasma biomarkers reflecting exercise adaptation and overload in racehorses. These novel candidates may enhance monitoring of performance, training status, and early signs of overtraining in equine athletes. This research was funded by the National Science Centre, Poland (NCN), under grant no. 2021/41/B/NZ7/03548.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The study included 49 active racehorses (37 Arabians, 12 Thoroughbreds; 15 mares, 33 stallions, 1 gelding), aged 2–7 years (median: 3). All were trained by the same professional under a standardised high-intensity regimen, housed individually with turnout access, and fed a consistent diet. Blood was collected during three training stages: T1 (n=49), T2 (n=44), and race phase (R, n=37). Samples were drawn at rest (p0), immediately post-exercise (p1), and after 30–40 min recovery (p2), yielding a total of 314 plasma samples for proteomics. Procedures complied with EU Directive 2010/63/EU and Polish law. An internal standard (IS) was prepared by pooling plasma from all horses. Albumin was depleted using a modified RAMP method on 5 µl of plasma. Reduced samples (TCEP) were centrifuged, and the supernatant was digested with a modified SP3 protocol using Sera-Mag beads. Beads were incubated with n-dodecyl β-D-maltoside and formic acid, then proteins were bound in acetonitrile, alkylated with MMTS, rebound, and washed. Proteins were digested overnight at 37 °C with trypsin in TEAB. Peptides were recovered by washing the beads, and concentrations were measured colorimetrically. Peptides (22 µg in 90 µl TEAB) from each sample were TMTpro 18plex-labelled using 385 µg of reagent in 40 µl ACN. In total, 19 TMTpro sets were prepared to analyse 314 individual samples and 19 IS samples; tag 126 was used for the IS in each set. After 1 h incubation and hydroxylamine quenching, labelling efficiency was confirmed via LC-MS. Peptides per set were combined, desalted on Oasis HLB cartridges, dried, and reconstituted in 10 mM ammonium hydroxide with 2% ACN for fractionation. High-pH reversed-phase chromatography was performed on an XBridge Peptide BEH C18 column (4.6 × 250 mm, 130 Å, 5 µm) using a Waters Acquity UPLC H-Class system. Mobile phases: A (H₂O), B (ACN), and 10% C (100 mM ammonium hydroxide) throughout. Gradient: 5–8% B (3 min), 8–15% (17 min), 15–25% (25 min), 25–33% (15 min), 33–50% (16 min), 50–90% (8 min), then 4 min at 90% and 2 min re-equilibration. Fractions were collected every minute (min 4–99), dried, and concatenated (1 with 65, 2 with 66, etc.), yielding 64 final fractions per TMTpro set. Each was reconstituted in 180 µl Evosep solvent A (0.1% FA in water) for LC-MS analysis. In total, 1216 LC-MS runs were performed. LC-MS analysis was performed using an Evosep One system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Scientific). Peptides (50 µl/fraction) were loaded onto Evotips C18 columns. Samples were washed and eluted using the 88 min preset gradient (15 samples/day) at 220 nl/min on an EV1106 analytical column (Dr Maisch C18 AQ, 1.9 µm, 150 µm ID × 15 cm). MS data were acquired in DDA mode. MS1 scans: resolution 60,000; AGC target 300%; scan range 300–1700 m/z; automatic injection time. MS2 scans: resolution 30,000; top 25 precursors; isolation window 1.2 m/z; dynamic exclusion 20 s; intensity threshold 5×10³; precursor fit ≥70%; HCD fragmentation at NCE 30%. TurboTMT mode was enabled for TMTpro quantification. Spray voltage: 2.1 kV; RF level: 40; capillary temperature: 275 °C.
dataProcessingProtocol: Offline recalibration, as well as peptide and protein identification, was performed using the MaxQuant/Andromeda software suite (version 2.5.0.0) [3], with the Equus caballus reference proteome (version 202504, one entry per gene) and the MaxQuant contaminants database. Searches were performed against tryptic peptides, with methylthio (C) specified as a fixed modification and oxidation (M) as a variable modification. Reporter MS2 TMTpro 18-plex quantification was enabled to allow peptide and protein-level quantitation. Target-decoy strategy was applied using a reversed database, and both peptide- and protein-level false discovery rates (FDR) were set to 1%. The “isobaric match between runs” option was enabled. Protein groups and quantitative data were further processed in Perseus (version 1.6.15) [4]. Reverse hits, contaminants, and proteins identified only by site were excluded. Data were normalised using the loading factor (LF) method: LF coefficients were calculated for each TMTpro channel by dividing the global median signal across all samples by the median signal in each channel, and individual protein intensities were then multiplied by the corresponding LF value. Log2 transformation was applied, and proteins identified in fewer than 50% of samples were filtered out. Remaining missing values were imputed from a normal distribution shifted toward the lower end of the intensity range to simulate low-abundance signals. Batch effects introduced by TMT set were corrected using the ComBat algorithm (R package), and correction performance was evaluated through distribution plots, Pearson correlation coefficients, and principal component analysis (PCA). Statistical analyses were performed using paired two-sample t-tests (horse-paired design) to compare samples collected before and after the exercise test across the full dataset, as well as within subgroups defined by horse breed, sex, and exercise type (training 1, training 2, race). Multiple hypothesis testing was corrected using FDR.
